title: Those sent forth
hook: by the winds sent forth one after another (77:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed al-Insan, and your line: morning and evening. Did the name of your Lord, or just a quiet pause, come at both ends of the day? Today a new surah, the last of the twenty-ninth part. Day six hundred sixty-two.

A cave in Mina, outside Mecca. A small group sits with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, one of his companions, later remembered it: a new surah was coming down, and the Prophet was reciting it, and Ibn Mas'ud was taking it fresh from his mouth. Then a snake slid out of the rock. They jumped for it. It got away. The Prophet said, more or less, it was spared your harm, as you were spared its harm. That's how al-Mursalat arrived, in a hadith in al-Bukhari. Surah seventy-seven. It opens with something that keeps coming.

Wal-mursalati 'urfa. By those sent forth, one after another. Al-mursalat comes from the root r-s-l, to send. It's the same root as rasul, a messenger, and risalah, a message. So the very first word of the surah is about sending. But sent forth what? The verse doesn't name them, and the commentators read it in more than one way. Many say the winds, gust after gust. Others say angels, sent down with Allah's commands. Some held both together. And 'urfan has two readings as well. One is one after another, like the hairs of a horse's mane, which is also called 'urf, lying in a row. The other is with kindness, from the same letters as ma'ruf, the good and decent thing. Then come five oaths in a run: those sent forth, those that blow hard, those that spread, those that separate, those that bring down a reminder. Five lines that sound like weather rolling in. And verse six says why the reminder comes: as an excuse or a warning. Verse seven lands the point: what you are promised will surely happen. Notice the pattern. Before the surah says anything about the Day to come, it points at something you've felt on your face. Wind doesn't arrive once. It keeps coming. The surah treats that as a sign: the One who keeps sending the wind keeps sending reminders too. Umm al-Fadl, the Prophet's aunt by marriage, said in another hadith that al-Mursalat was the last surah she heard him recite, at the sunset prayer, near the end of his life. A surah about things that keep coming, and it kept being recited to the end.

The practice: notice one thing that keeps coming. Sit where you are. Close your eyes or lower them. Listen first. Is there something that repeats? A fan, traffic, a clock, wind against a window, a neighbor's footsteps. If the room is silent, there's still one: your breath. In, out, and in again, without your asking. Pick one and stay with it. Each time it comes back, let it count as one more arrival. You don't have to name it as anything else. Just notice that it keeps being sent. The bell holds the time.
Those sent forth. Al-mursalat, from r-s-l, the root of messenger: winds or angels, sent one after another, the first word of surah seventy-seven. Today's word.
Your line: sent forth. Today, when a gust of wind or a repeated sound catches you, let it be a small reminder that arrived on time. Day six hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Al-Mursalat is a short Meccan surah recited in prayer; many Muslims know its opening oaths by heart, and commentators have long discussed whether its first verses describe winds, angels or both.

fork.reveal: in the hadith in al-Bukhari, he lets it go with a line about harm avoided on both sides.

original.note: Arabic, 77:1: by those sent forth, one after another.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old oath about the wind.
what it means: by those sent forth one after another, winds or angels, a sign that reminders keep coming.
what a scholar hears: mursalat shares r-s-l with rasul; 'urfan can mean in a row, like a mane, or with kindness, like ma'ruf.
